The human login is the load-bearing third case: it passes through untouched, so nobody is normalised into looking like a reviewer.
  • The REVIEW_THREADS_REQUIRE_RESOLVED flag has three claims, one test each (#544): three different verdicts, not one assertion over three inputs; collapsing them hid the third. CI no longer passes False (#196): delegating the resolve half to required_conversation_resolution looked safe, but that setting drops an outdated thread (#193: merge enabled over an unresolved outdated thread with 29 of 29 checks green). The flag survives for callers that cannot re-evaluate a resolve, so the reply-only mode must keep working and must not quietly disable the job altogether.
  • A redundant re-review is not an unreviewed PR (#259). The reviewer's boilerplate is copied verbatim from #264's own comment stream; it is appended to every outcome (performed, rate-limited and failed alike), which is what defeated the first draft of the check.
  • Real notice bodies, never retyped (#364, #433). The chat-quota notice (PR #363, 2026-08-30T18:44:28Z), the review-quota notice (PR #317, 2026-08-29T17:11:51Z) and the file-cap notice (PR #424, 2026-09-11) are fetched with gh api graphql; the issue the first closed was itself written against retyped text that classified differently from the real bytes. A second, unrelated "Review skipped" reason (measured on PR #400, a one-file bot-authored PR, clearable simply by asking, unlike the structural cap) shares the bare prefix with the file-cap notice, which is what makes it a genuine negative control. The bot suffix is stripped first, or the notice lookup silently finds nothing.
  • Classification by declared structure (#630, docs/faq.md). Each shape is a trimmed copy of a real body from this repo's PRs (#347, #671 to #687), and the witness is the same text with only its structural marker removed. The real CodeRabbit body from #347 has its only finding in a body section, not an inline thread.
  • The display budget must not reach a matcher (#372). summarise_reviewer_notice cuts a notice to 200 characters so a failure message stays readable. Two matchers used to read that cut string, so a phrase past the budget read as absent. Over 112 real reviewer notices, 4 flipped UNKNOWN to OK (phrase at offsets 394, 583, 583 and 2700) and 4 lost a completion phrase; both directions are silent.
  • A review carries forward across a merge of the base (#698). The patch-id output is <patch-id> <commit-id>, and unpacking fails loudly on empty output instead of an IndexError. The merge of main into the branch conflicts by design.

docs.title: Dependabot auto-merge
docs.text: Dependabot PRs merge themselves when CI proves them safe. The same policy runs on BlueprintX and in every generated project, from one implementation: templates/common/bin/dependabot_auto_merge.sh and templates/common/.github/workflows/dependabot-auto-merge.yml. BlueprintX's own workflow runs that script directly; generated projects get a copy at scaffold time.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text:
Update Review required Merges patch, minor no on green, via native squash auto-merge major yes, on the current head on green, once reviewed

A Dependabot diff is a version string and a lockfile, so a review of a patch or minor bump has nothing to read, and CodeRabbit skips bot PRs. CI builds each template and runs its own lint and tests, which is the real check. Majors can break a template in ways that need judgement, so they keep the review.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. dependabot/fetch-metadata (pinned by SHA) reports every dependency's updateType. A grouped PR counts as major if any member is.
  2. dependabot_auto_merge.sh re-checks that the PR author and every commit are dependabot[bot], then arms auto-merge for patch/minor. For a major it arms only when someone other than Dependabot reviewed the current head; otherwise it waits. Whenever it does not arm (a human commit, an unreviewed major, a rebase that superseded the review), it also disables auto-merge, so a PR armed at an earlier head never merges on stale approval. A submitted or dismissed review re-triggers the job (pull_request_review), so a reviewed major merges on green without a manual re-run.
  3. The Review threads answered gate (check_review_threads.py) skips its "a declared reviewer must have reported" check for a PR that is dependabot (a Bot), whose every commit is authored by Dependabot, and whose commit metadata (update-type:) is only patch or minor. Threads are still checked.

docs.title: Fail-closed
docs.text:
Each of these removes the exemption, and the PR needs a review as usual:

  • the update type is major, missing or unparsable (decided from metadata, never the title);
  • the author is not Dependabot;
  • any commit is not Dependabot's, so a human push voids it (@dependabot rebase restores it);
  • the PR has more than 100 commits (checked by the review gate only).

The workflow uses pull_request_target because one trigger then covers Dependabot opens and pushes with a write token, and the review event runs the same code. It never checks out PR code; the script comes from the base commit.

docs.title: What counts as a Dependabot commit
docs.text:
Commit metadata proves nothing about who pushed: web-flow signs every web-editor and API commit, and the author is a field any write-access user can set. So the rule has two layers:

  1. Who pushed. On a pull_request_target event the sender must be dependabot[bot]. On a review event, and in the review-thread gate, every pull_request workflow run on the head commit must have been started by dependabot[bot] (REST actions/runs?head_sha=..., the run's actor; a re-run by a human does not change it). A human push, an unreadable result, no run, or a truncated list all fail closed. A non-Dependabot synchronize also disables auto-merge, and it stays off until Dependabot pushes again.
  2. What was pushed. Every commit has author dependabot[bot], committer web-flow and a verified signature (the gate reads GraphQL signature.isValid with signer web-flow).

A merge commit from the "Update branch" button fails both layers; @dependabot rebase restores the PR.

docs.title: Who counts as a reviewer
docs.text:
A public repo accepts reviews from any account, so a review counts toward a major only when it is on the current head, in state APPROVED or COMMENTED, and comes from one of:

  • a human (user.type is not Bot) whose author_association is OWNER, MEMBER or COLLABORATOR;
  • a reviewer bot: user.type is Bot and the exact login is a posts: threads entry in .review-bots.yaml (for example coderabbitai[bot] and the reviewer-ladder App).

The roster is read from the PR's base branch through the contents API, never from the PR head, so a commit on the Dependabot branch cannot add itself to it. A User account named like a roster bot does not count, nor does a posts: status member such as github-actions[bot]. A trusted CHANGES_REQUESTED on the head blocks. The job gates on the PR author, never the actor (on a review event the actor is the reviewer), and arms with --match-head-commit so GitHub refuses if the head moved after the check. The review-thread exemption never counts reviews, so it needs no such filter.

docs.title: Unverified until a real major is reviewed
docs.text: The review-triggered run is untested against a live Dependabot major. Whether the token of a pull_request_review run may arm auto-merge on a Dependabot PR is not verified; if it cannot, the job fails visibly and the fallback is re-running it from the Actions tab.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: tests/test_dependabot_auto_merge.sh stubs gh; the Dependabot cases in templates/python-common/tests/unit/test_review_threads_gate.py cover the gate. Both pin the should-fail cases: major, non-Dependabot author, human commit, and a grouped PR with one major.

docs.title: Behaviours to know
docs.text:
• A human reopen does not re-arm: reopened is not a trigger, so the PR waits for the next Dependabot push (@dependabot rebase) or a qualifying review.
  • A human labeled or edited run on the head commit also counts as "not pushed by Dependabot" in the pusher lookup, because the API has no event-action filter. That fails closed: the PR needs a review or @dependabot rebase.
  • A reviewer-bot COMMENTED review can arm a major, but arming only queues the merge. The required Review threads answered check still fails while the ladder's body findings are unanswered (blueprintx#630), so nothing merges unread.
  • Auto-merge needs "Allow auto-merge" and required status checks on the repository; without them --auto fails or merges immediately.
  • The pusher lookup needs at least one pull_request workflow run on the head commit. A repository whose CI only runs on push or skips lockfile-only diffs gets no exemption and no major ever arms; this fails closed.
  • A failed --disable-auto fails the job (only "not enabled" is ignored), so a PR armed at an earlier head never stays armed behind a green run.
  • The roster is read at the base commit SHA. Reviews are collapsed to each trusted reviewer's latest state, so an approval after a change request arms, and a standing block from an earlier head still blocks.
  • The review-triggered run uses the workflow file from the PR's merge ref. It runs only after a review is submitted, and a Dependabot bump of this workflow's own pins is part of the diff that review covers.
  • The roster parser expects - login: before posts: inside an entry, as the shipped .review-bots.yaml writes it; an entry in another order is ignored, so that bot never counts.
  • Runs are serialised per PR (concurrency, newest wins), so a late run on an old head cannot disarm what a newer run armed.

docs.title: Dependabot configuration
docs.text:
Every skeleton ships a .github/dependabot.yml when a GitHub remote is connected (the offline mode removes .github/, so it ships none there). The root repository's own .github/dependabot.yml follows the same rules.

Family Source Ecosystems Python (six skeletons) templates/python-common/.github/dependabot.yml pip (lockfile-only), github-actions TypeScript (react-spa-webpack, ts-lib) templates/ts-common/dependabot.yml npm, github-actions Bash (bash-cli, etcher-chromeos, ventoy-usb) templates/common/.github/dependabot.yml github-actions

docs.title: Cooldown
docs.text:
A release is aged before Dependabot proposes it. Security updates ignore the cooldown.

  • pip and npm: semver-patch-days: 3, semver-minor-days: 7, semver-major-days: 90 (90 is the schema maximum, range 1-90).
  • github-actions: default-days: 7; it does not support the semver-* keys.

docs.title: Lint stack
docs.text: eslint, @eslint/js, typescript-eslint and eslint-plugin-jest share one eslint group in every npm block, so the lint stack moves as a unit. A lone @eslint/js major once broke npm ci with ERESOLVE. The templates are on eslint 10 (#839), so no major is ignored.

docs.title: Gate
docs.text: bin/ci/check_dependabot_shipped.sh --static (pre-commit hook dependabot-shipped, CI job dependabot-shipped) fails when a skeleton script stops copying dependabot.yml, copies a file that does not exist, or the copied file sets no cooldown. There is no --generated mode: the default scaffold answers take the offline path, which removes .github/, so a generated tree would never contain the file.

docs.title: Docs boundary gate
docs.text: bin/ci/check_docs_boundary.sh (blueprintx#536, extended to generated projects by #576) fails when docs/ holds working material instead of published documentation. BlueprintX runs it on its own tree; every generated Python project gets a copy at bin/check_docs_boundary.sh and runs it with --root . in pre-commit and CI.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
Everything under docs/ must be published documentation. Anything else is redirected to the place that owns it:

Found in docs/ Belongs in backlog/ .specs/backlog/; reader-facing content goes to README.md / CONTRIBUTING.md a file whose name contains lesson outside docs/; a lesson hardened into a rule goes to CONTRIBUTING.md as the rule design.md, plan.md .specs/features/<feature-name>/ (#447) security.md, threat*.md the root SECURITY.md (GitHub only reads it from the root, .github/ or the docs/ root) any .superpowers* path segment that tool's own home

The list is open: when a new kind of working material appears, add the case and its destination.

docs.title: Design notes
docs.text:
• A denied directory is reported once and not descended into.
  • A bad --root fails: otherwise every later check would see "no docs/" and report success.
  • A missing docs/ is not an error: the gate exits 0 with "nothing to check".
  • Git-ignored entries are skipped, but only when --root is itself a repository top level, and with global git config disabled so local and CI verdicts agree.
  • Symlinks are classified, then treated as leaves: following them re-enters the tree through longer paths.
  • An unreadable docs/ or subdirectory, or an empty docs/, fails: a check that cannot see its subject has not passed.
  • From the BlueprintX root the gate never walks templates/*/docs/; those are skeleton content, verified by running the gate inside a generated project (bin/ci/scaffold_lint_test.sh).

Worked, end-to-end walkthroughs of the skeletons BlueprintX scaffolds. Each links into the relevant skeleton's own example set.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Common questions about using and extending BlueprintX.

See also: Get Started · CLI Reference · Contributing.

docs.title: What is BlueprintX?
docs.text: A Make + bash scaffolding tool that generates opinionated Python and TypeScript project skeletons (DDD service, MVC service, minimal library, React SPA) with CI, pre-commit, tests, and docs wired in. It is not a Python application — the Python code lives in templates/ and is copied into scaffolded projects.

docs.title: How do I scaffold a project?
docs.text: make new, then answer the prompts (language → skeleton → project name). See Get Started.

docs.title: How do I add a new skeleton?
docs.text: Create templates/<name>/ with a skeleton.meta descriptor, add a scaffold script under bin/scaffold/, and the menu discovers it automatically. See Contributing.

docs.title: Do I need a global git identity to scaffold?
docs.text: No. The scaffold's commits use your user.name / user.email (or the GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL / GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL environment variables) when set. When none of these is configured it commits as BlueprintX Scaffold <scaffold@blueprintx.invalid> for those commits only, prints a one-line notice, and never writes the fallback to any git config. Set your own identity later with git config --global user.name "Your Name" and git config --global user.email "you@example.com".

docs.title: Online vs offline scaffolds — what's the difference?
docs.text: If you connect a GitHub remote, the scaffold ships GitHub-only assets (Actions workflows, CODEOWNERS, PR template). Without one, it ships an offline git-diff workflow instead. Library projects also switch versioning: online = tag-driven, offline = a local poe bump_version (cz bump, run inside the generated project — not a BlueprintX make target).

docs.title: I don't use a PR review bot — will the generated project's required check ever pass?
docs.text: The scaffolder asks "Do you have (or will you install) a PR review bot such as CodeRabbit on this repo?". Answer no and it skips copying .review-bots.yaml instead of shipping it empty — reviewers: [] is treated by the gate as "switched off from inside the very PR it polices" and raises, which is worse than never having adopted the gate at all. With the file absent, check_review_threads.py reads "the review-thread gate is not adopted here" and exits 0: the required check still runs on every PR (nothing else changes in .github/), it just reports success instead of demanding a reviewer that will never exist. Answer yes later and re-adding the roster turns the gate back on — at the path the gate reads, which differs by language: for Python copy templates/python-common/.review-bots.yaml to the project root; for TypeScript copy templates/ts-common/.github/.review-bots.yaml to .github/.review-bots.yaml. See blueprintx#374 (why this needed a fix) and blueprintx#262 (why an empty roster is not the opt-out).

docs.title: How does a fallback (ladder) review satisfy the gate?
docs.text: A roster row with kind: comment-marker and a marker: string (here Fallback review — runtime:) lets a plain issue comment count as a review. The comment must start with the marker, name the head SHA on its second line (Reviewed head: <sha>), be posted after the head commit, and be authored by a login listed in the row's posters: (the ladder App, e.g. guilhermegor-review-ladder[bot]; [bot] is normalised like roster logins, and the author must also be a GitHub Bot actor, so a user registering the bare name does not match). GitHub's authorAssociation is deliberately NOT consulted: the PR author is usually the repo OWNER, so trusting the association let the author self-approve by typing the marker (blueprintx#761). An empty or missing posters: accepts no marker. The row has no login: and is ignored when absent. The comment must also contain the line 0 finding(s) across N reviewed file(s).; a count above zero, or no such line, fails closed, so a ladder review with findings never satisfies the gate on its own (blueprintx#630). Like a clean-review notice, it proves a review ran, never that a thread was answered. The workflow needs the issue_comment trigger to re-run on that comment (created, edited or deleted). A run triggered by a comment reports on the default branch's head, not the PR's, so a red "Review threads answered" on main's tip after such a comment is that run's own verdict, not a broken main; the PR's check is refreshed by the stale-run step. The Python roster (templates/python-common/.review-bots.yaml) and the TypeScript one (templates/ts-common/.github/.review-bots.yaml, workflow review-threads.yml) both ship the row and the trigger. See blueprintx#593.

docs.title: How does a scaffolded repo close the issue a merged PR delivered?
docs.text:
Every generated project with a GitHub remote receives close-linked-issues.yml and its bin/close_linked_issues.sh (blueprintx#604). Offline scaffolds get neither: their only consumers are the removed workflows.

GitHub's own Closes #N linking can come back empty (a Closes: #N with a colon, or a merge that did not link), which leaves the issue open and keeps a Projects "Item closed" -> Done automation from firing. On a merged same-repo PR into the default branch the workflow closes, matching strictly (a wrong closure is worse than a missed one). A PR merged into another branch (a stacked PR) closes nothing, because the work has not reached the default branch. Merges made with the default GITHUB_TOKEN (an auto-merge or merge-queue action) never trigger pull_request: closed, so only merges by a person, an App token or a PAT are covered:

  • the issue number in a branch named <type>/<N>-<slug>, where the type is feat, feature, fix, bugfix, hotfix, docs, refactor, chore or test and N is not a year-month date (feat/12-add-thing closes issue 12; feat/1999-x closes 1999; chore/2026-10-cleanup and fix/python-3-12 close nothing, and a trailing -N is never read). A real issue number that looks like a year-month, such as feat/2010-12-factor-app, is skipped too: a miss, never a wrong closure;
  • each Closes #N, Fixes #N or Resolves #N pair in the PR body (GitHub's closing keywords close, fix and resolve in their -s/-d/-es forms; colon allowed), at a word boundary. Closes #1, #2 closes only #1. Like GitHub's own linker, it ignores fenced code blocks, inline code, > quotes and <!-- --> comments. A negated use is ignored, also across a line break: not, never, cannot, n't, no longer, revert(s|ed|ing) or without, followed by up to three words and the keyword ("does not fully fix #12", "this reverts the change that fixes #8"). Any other wording, such as "I doubt this fixes #8", still closes.

It skips the whole PR, branch and body alike, for dependabot/*, renovate/* and release/* branches (their bodies quote upstream Fixes #N text, and a trailing -4 is a version). It also skips the PR's own number, any number that is a PR, and owner/repo#N references, which point at another repository. A fork PR is skipped too: its token is read-only. A missing issue (HTTP 404, or 410 for a deleted issue or a repo with Issues disabled) is skipped; any other API error fails the job, and one failed close does not stop the others. The branch name and PR body are untrusted text and reach the script only through env:. It complements, and does not replace, the Projects "Item closed -> Done" workflow. It is dropped with the rest of .github/ in offline mode.

docs.title: The scaffolder offered me a kanban board and labels — what does it do?
docs.text:
After it creates the GitHub repo, the scaffolder creates the house labels (type:task, type:research, type:grilling, hitl, afk, oracle:strong, oracle:weak, do-not-merge) and asks whether to create a <repo> kanban GitHub Project. Answer yes and it creates the board, links it to the repo, sets Status to Backlog / Ready / In progress / In review / Done, and adds Priority, Size, Estimate, Start date, Target date and Points. Visibility defaults to the repo's own.

It is safe to re-run: labels use --force, an existing <repo> kanban board is skipped, and two boards with that title are reported, never guessed between. A token without the project scope prints gh auth refresh -s project and scaffolding carries on. Views and the built-in workflows (auto-add items, item closed to Done) have no public API, so enable them at the URL the scaffolder prints (.../projects/<n>/workflows).

docs.title: How is BlueprintX itself versioned?
docs.text: The version is the git tag. Cut a release from the Release GitHub Action (enter the version once); blueprintx --version resolves it via git describe from a checkout, or a stamped literal for a packaged install. See the Changelog.

docs.title: Does a review that only has a body need an answer?
docs.text: Yes. A roster reviewer that posts findings as the review body, with no inline thread, used to satisfy Review threads answered unread, because the gate only counted threads (16 PRs merged that way on 2026-10-05, blueprintx#630). The gate does not parse prose to guess; it classifies a comment by the structure the comment declares for itself, and when that is ambiguous it counts the comment as a review, so a valid review is never dropped.

docs.title: How the gate classifies a review
docs.text:
A roster author's review (on any commit, as threads are; a DISMISSED one is skipped) or issue comment is a review when it has one of these shapes. A roster issue comment counts only with the ladder attribution line or a CodeRabbit header, so a status notice such as Review ladder: all rungs failed is not a review. A printed count wins over everything else:

  • CodeRabbit's body sections Outside diff range comments (N) and Duplicate comments (N) with N > 0: these live only in the body, so they need a reply even when Actionable comments posted: 0;
  • Actionable comments posted: N alone: the N findings are inline threads, which the thread check already holds (reply and resolve), so the body needs no extra reply for them;
  • N finding(s) across M reviewed file(s) at the start of a line (the ladder posts no threads): 0 is clean, N > 0 needs a reply;
  • the ladder attribution line Fallback review — runtime: <x>, model: <y> (selected by: <z>) without a count (the claude rung writes prose): a review, unless the prose is only No findings.;
  • a Review or Findings heading, bullet, bold label or Review: line, and numbered Finding 1: items;
  • a severity emoji, Major/Critical/Minor/Blocker opening a line as bold, in brackets or before :/a dash, Severity: <word>, or a count that opens a line (2 finding(s)).

A line that is only No findings., Review: no findings, Minor: none or None. (and a heading directly followed by one) is clean. Nitpick and Trivial lines never need a reply. CodeRabbit's walkthrough, rate-limit and command-reply comments are not reviews because of their SHAPE: they carry no ladder attribution line, Actionable header or body section, and a roster issue comment counts as a review only with one of those.

Count authority binds to the author, not the body: the Actionable header only speaks for CodeRabbit, and the N finding(s) across count only for the ladder app and only with its attribution line. Any other author's counts are ignored and its body is read by structure, so quoting a header never clears findings. Quoted lines and fenced blocks are ignored too.

Missing or unrecognised input fails closed: a body section with no parsable count, a ladder attribution with nothing after it, and a review comment with no timestamp all count as findings; only an explicit clean statement or a stated 0 clears a review. Issue comments, reviews and threads are all paginated, so a PR with 140 comments is read in full; a page that fails to load fails the check instead of shortening the list.

docs.title: When the gate runs, and which marker wins
docs.text:
A clean review and a ladder fallback review arrive only as issue comments, so the workflow also listens to issue_comment, and deleted re-runs the gate when such a comment is removed. Those runs report on the default branch's head; the pull request's own required check is refreshed by the stale-run step. issue_comment also fires for plain issues, where there is no pull request to audit.

When several trusted review markers exist, the latest one decides before the Reviewed head: line is checked. A later marker with a missing or garbled head line fails closed instead of falling back to an earlier marker.

docs.title: How the gate classifies an answer
docs.text: An answer comes from outside the reviewer roster, is a user account (not a bot, app, organization or deleted ghost), and is posted after the review. It counts when it is either 100 characters or longer, or has an answer shape at any length: a line that opens with Reply to review <id>, Answer(s) to ... review, Re: review, Verdicts/Judgment on the ... review, or a review <id> citation, Addressed in <sha>/Fixed in <sha>, a Finding N: heading, or a > quoted finding followed by a response. A review request (@coderabbitai re-review, Ready for re-review) or a status line (Not answered yet) is neither. One reply after the latest review answers the earlier ones; a body has no thread, so nothing needs resolving. When threads are also open, the failure lists both. Re-run the check after replying. The tests in test_review_threads_gate.py list every shape with a witness that fails without its marker. The rule is weaker than a thread: a long comment answers without being tied to a finding.

docs.title: When does a review still count after the branch moves?
docs.text:
A review is pinned to the commit it was written against. When no review names the head, the gate asks whether the PR's own patch changed between the reviewed commit R and the head H. If it did not, the review covers H and the gate prints review at R still covers H: the head only merges the base, the PR's own patch is unchanged. That is the case of update-branch under the strict-serial ruleset: main is merged in, no code is written, and a second review of the same diff would only spend a reviewer rung.

The patch is the diff from the merge base with the base branch to the commit. It is fingerprinted from what the PR authored: the file name, status and previous name, and the ordered +/- lines with all whitespace. Hunk headers (coordinates and function context) and unchanged context lines are dropped, because they describe the base: a merge of main that adds a function next to the PR's lines splits one hunk into two with different headers, and the PR's own lines did not change. This is stricter than git patch-id --stable, which also normalises whitespace. The CI checkout is shallow (actions/checkout defaults to fetch-depth: 1), so there is no local history for git merge-base; the gate reads the same diff from the GitHub compare API (compare/<base>...<commit>), which computes the merge base server side.

Both compares name the base by the commit SHA read once with the PR, never by branch name, so a retarget or a push to the base between the two reads cannot make them measure different bases. The head is fingerprinted once, by the caller, and handed to each comparison, so the guarantee does not rest on the compare function caching anything: if the head cannot be read the comparison stops there. Reviewed commits are tried newest first and at most five of them (_INT_MAX_REVIEWED_COMMITS: a PR reviewed at more commits than that is simply re-reviewed), so a PR makes at most six compare calls. The retarget check below reads the same GraphQL response as the reviews, so it adds no call of its own; a test pins the worst case, six calls at the timeout below, to half of the shortest job timeout (10 minutes). A pass that rests on a carried-forward review is shown in the verdict: one line in the normal output, and a carried_forward_from field (the reviewed commit) under --json, where stdout stays one document. The check runs after the completion-notice check, so a PR that already passes makes no compare call. Each call has a 20 second timeout, and a timeout, a missing gh or an API error all read as "not covered", with one line on stderr per failing commit giving the reason (stdout stays the --json document). A DISMISSED review is never carried forward. Every review's findings, threads or body, are audited afterwards whatever the carry-forward decided.

What carries forward is therefore narrower than "any update-branch". A conflict-free base edit anywhere, including next to or inside a hunk's three context lines, leaves the fingerprint alone, since only the PR's own +/- lines count. The tests pin this against real git diff output. Known ceilings: an identical edit moved to another function matches, because hunk headers are not hashed (the trade-off of blueprintx#848; git patch-id ignores headers too); and a conflict-free base change can still break the unchanged patch semantically (main renames a function the PR calls), which a patch comparison cannot see. That is accepted: a review is repeated only when a conflict or new code changes the PR's own patch, and CI covers the integration. A PR from a fork whose commits cannot be compared fails closed like any other error.

A review submitted before the PR's latest base change gets no carry-forward. The compare measures the patch against today's base, which need not be the base such a review was written against, so the same fingerprint proves nothing. A review submitted after that change was written against the current base lineage, so it carries through a merge-only update like on any other PR (blueprintx#809). The gate looks for a BASE_REF_CHANGED_EVENT or AUTOMATIC_BASE_CHANGE_SUCCEEDED_EVENT timeline item (the second is what GitHub records when it retargets a PR itself after its base branch is merged and deleted) in the same GraphQL query as the reviews, reads each event's createdAt, and refuses a review whose submittedAt is not strictly later than the newest one. When one commit has several live reviews from the roster, the newest decides, so a post-change review supersedes an earlier one on the same commit. An event is never removed, so a review older than it stays refused permanently. The gate prints the reason on stderr, and every unreadable answer fails closed: a missing event list ("retarget state is unknown"), an event or review without a parseable time, and a review that is not later than the event are all refused, never read as "never retargeted". The gate reads the filtered nodes, never totalCount, which ignores the type filter and counts the whole timeline. A stacked PR whose lower PR merged was retargeted automatically, so a review from before that retarget needs a fresh one.

Still superseded, so a new review is needed: a merge that resolves a conflict, any new commit, and a force-push that rewrites the code, because each changes the fingerprint. The gate fails closed: a missing commit, an API error, a malformed response (files not a list, an entry that is not an object, a non-JSON body), a binary or oversized file with no patch text, or a full 300-file list is read as "not covered". A pure rename (status renamed, zero changes) has no patch text by nature and is fingerprinted by its two names and its blob sha, so it carries forward. The sha is required: a binary file also reports zero changes, and only its blob proves the content. The compare API returns at most 300 files whatever per_page says (it pages commits, not files), so a list that long may be cut off. The gate asks for per_page=1 to keep the commit list, which it does not use, small.

docs.title: Why does every scaffold have to ship the hosted-reviewer config?
docs.text:
Every generated project must ship the configuration for the hosted reviewers (CodeRabbit, Greptile and Graphite); today only Graphite's is listed. Left as a copy list maintained by hand in nine scaffold scripts, that drifts: MVC once silently lacked shared files (poetry.toml, .coveragerc). The required paths are listed once, one bare path per line (blank and # lines are ignored), in templates/common/review-config.manifest, and bin/ci/check_review_config_shipped.sh checks them in three modes:

  • --static (pre-commit hook review-config-shipped): every manifest path exists under templates/common/, and every skeleton script discovered from templates/*/skeleton.meta has a cp that copies it (a loop or an unusual copy is a documented limit; --generated covers it).
  • --generated (CI job review-config-shipped): scaffolds each discovered skeleton with its default answers and asserts every manifest path is in the generated tree. This is the real oracle: a cp line that sits behind a branch the default answers never take passes --static and fails here. --skeleton <name> narrows it to one.
  • --project <dir> (called by scaffold_lint_test.sh for each Python tier): the same assertion over one already-generated project.

templates/common/review-config.manifest is the list of guarded paths; the PR that ships a reviewer config file adds its path there, so read the file rather than this page. These are repo-root files, not GitHub-only assets, so the offline scaffold keeps them: apply_offline_mode drops only .github/.

--static is a fast heuristic over direct cp commands. It reads the scaffold script plus the bin/lib/*.sh helpers it sources, resolves the *_TEMPLATE_ROOT variables, and accepts a path only when a cp takes exactly templates/common/<path> into a destination ending in <path>, or a recursive copy (-r, -R, -a, --recursive) of templates/common or one of its parent directories. Comments, backup files, another template root and unrelated parent directories do not count. It cannot follow a copy whose source is built at run time (a for loop over a variable, say), so such a script fails --static even when it ships the file. That is the safe direction: write the copy out directly, or rely on --generated.

Every project ships the config, offline ones included, because an offline project can later be promoted to GitHub. scaffold_lint_test.sh only forbids four GitHub-only workflow files in an offline project, none of which is reviewer config.

The manifest only grows: the change that ships a reviewer config file adds that file's path to the manifest in the same pull request. check_content in the script is the hook point for content checks, such as keeping Greptile queue-only. tests/test_check_review_config_shipped.sh removes a cp line, a manifest file and an unshipped entry from a copy of the tree and shows the gate going red in both modes.

docs.title: Which install methods are supported?
docs.text: Homebrew, Chocolatey, Snap, apt, and make install from a clone — see the project README.

docs.title: 1. Clone the repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/guilhermegor/blueprintx.git
cd blueprintx

docs.title: 2. Run the interactive scaffolder
docs.text:
make new         # interactive scaffolder
make preview     # show skeleton structures
make dev         # scaffold into a temp dir (kept)
make dev_clean   # scaffold into temp dir and auto-delete on exit
make dry_run     # print structure; no files written

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• bash ≥ 4
  • For Python skeletons: pyenv + poetry (or your Python toolchain of choice) in the generated project
  • For TypeScript skeletons: the Node.js floor is ^22.18.0 || >=24.11.0 for ts-lib and ^22.22.0 || >=24.11.0 for react-spa-webpack (react-router 8 raises it); ts-lib's floor is the range Babel 8 requires (each declares its own engines.node); run npm install after scaffolding

docs.title: ✨ Highlights
docs.text:
• Interactive CLI (make new) with auto-discovered language and skeleton menus
  • Python skeletons: DDD service (hexagonal/ports-and-adapters, native DB or SQLAlchemy ORM), MVC service (layered, script/pipeline style, native DB or SQLAlchemy ORM), and lib-minimal
  • TypeScript skeletons: React SPA with Webpack 5, Babel, ESLint, and Prettier
  • Common Python baseline: templated pyproject.toml, pre-commit, VS Code settings, CI workflow, CODEOWNERS, PR template, and test folders
  • Common TypeScript baseline: package.json with pinned deps, .gitignore, VS Code settings, CONTRIBUTING.md
  • Dev/preview modes: temp scaffolds, dry-run structure previews, optional auto-clean
  • Extensible: add a skeleton.meta to any templates/ directory and it appears in the menu automatically

📦 GitHub Repository: github.com/guilhermegor/blueprintx

docs.title: Graphite Configuration
docs.text: Graphite has no repo-level config file (no .graphite.yaml). Everything below is either one versioned file or a dashboard step the repository owner performs by hand.

docs.title: What the repository versions
docs.text:
• .gitattributes marks lockfiles and the coverage badge linguist-generated=true. The comment-budget baseline is deliberately not marked: it is a ratchet, and a reviewer must see its count go up. Per Graphite's docs, marked files are collapsed in the Graphite and GitHub diff views, skipped by the AI review and excluded from its PR size check. They are collapsed for every reviewer and human too.
  • The review rules are the existing .greptile/rules.md. There is no .graphite/ copy.

docs.title: Dashboard steps (not versionable)
docs.text:
1. Install the Graphite GitHub App on the account (personal accounts: Join team), then sync the repository.
  2. AI reviews, enable the repository.
  3. Rules & exclusions, add a file-based rule with the glob .greptile/rules.md (globs are case-sensitive; large files are truncated).
  4. Settings tab (org-admin rights required), PR filtering by PR labels: restrict AI reviews to PRs carrying review:graphite.

docs.title: Never auto-review
docs.text: Graphite reviews every new PR by default. The label filter in step 4 is the opt-in: the /dev-loop ladder adds review:graphite when it is Graphite's turn and removes it once the review lands. A label left on lets every push trigger another review.

docs.title: Measured behavior
docs.text:
Measured on blueprintx#807, 2026-10-16.

  • Adding the label is enough. At 10:25:13 UTC the label was added to head 8912317c with no push and no comment; about 76 s later Graphite reported the check run Graphite / AI Reviews (app graphite-app): success, "AI review ran and left 0 comments".
  • A clean review leaves no PR review and no comment. The check run is its only trace, so a review-thread gate that counts reviews sees nothing.
  • Without the label, nothing runs. Heads ac0f9231 and 5d3e1fde, pushed while the label was absent, each got the check run Graphite / AI Reviews with conclusion skipped ("does not match your org's AI review filters") and zero reviews.

Login measured on 2026-10-17 (probe PR with deliberate defects, label review:graphite added at 21:43:12 UTC): about 67 s later Graphite / AI Reviews reported "AI review ran and left 2 comments", and graphite-app[bot] (type Bot) submitted a COMMENTED review carrying 2 inline review comments. So .review-bots.yaml lists it as posts: threads. A draft PR got nothing in 10 minutes, so the label only works on a PR that is ready for review.

docs.title: In BlueprintX itself
docs.text: The BlueprintX root has no .greptile/rules.md (each skeleton ships its own, under templates/<skeleton>/.greptile/). The file-based rule for this repository points at CLAUDE.md instead. The ship check for the shared page is bin/ci/check_review_config_shipped.sh, which lists it in templates/common/review-config.manifest.

docs.title: Issue scope: declaring and enforcing a file surface
docs.text: blueprintx#314. Turns the hand-written "collision map" every dispatched agent used to get — a prose list of files currently in flight, reconstructed from memory on every dispatch, never checked — into something a gate can read and verify at PR time.

docs.title: The problem this replaces
docs.text: Two agents given isolation: "worktree" once ended up touching the same directory: one agent's files were wiped mid-task, an empty commit reported full success, and a foreign commit leaked onto another agent's branch. The prose collision map that was supposed to prevent this was reconstructed by hand every dispatch, only as good as the orchestrator's recall, and nothing verified an agent actually respected it.

docs.title: Declaration format: a fenced surface block, not a scope:* label
docs.text:
The issue's own proposal was a scope:<area> label (scope:templates-python, scope:bin-ci, …). This gate uses a fenced code block in the issue body instead:

```surface
bin/ci/check_issue_scope.py
docs/issue-scope.md
```

One path or glob per line. A path matches an entry either exactly, or via shell-style wildcards (fnmatch) — * already spans /, so docs/* and docs/** match the same set; either spelling is accepted for readability. Lines starting with # are comments.

Why not the label. A label needs a second artifact to mean anything: a taxonomy file mapping each scope:* value to the paths it actually names, kept in sync with the milestone structure by hand. The issue's own scope section already names the risk: "backfilling ~40 issues by hand is where this quietly dies." A fenced block sidesteps both problems — it is the declaration (no separate mapping to maintain), and it is opt-in per issue rather than a mass rewrite of every open issue on day one. It also mirrors a pattern already live in this repo's own dispatch loop: the orchestrator's dispatch-claims.tsv is exactly <issue>\t<path> lines, one path per claim.

Labels remain available for coarse routing (oracle:*, hitl/afk) where "which bucket" is the question. This gate answers a different, finer question — "which exact paths" — where a label's blast-radius granularity is the wrong shape.

docs.title: What the check compares
docs.text: The set of files a PR touches must be a subset of the union of the surface patterns declared on every issue the PR closes (closingIssuesReferences — not the PR body's "Closes #N" text, the resolved GitHub reference, since only that reflects whether the PR actually targets the default branch and therefore whether the reference is live at all).

docs.title: Call budget
docs.text: This session's GitHub API quota was exhausted three times in one day by checks that re-query every open PR and branch. This gate is deliberately frugal: the PR's changed files, its closingIssuesReferences, and its commits (for the override trailer, below) come back from one gh pr view --json files,closingIssuesReferences,commits call — closingIssuesReferences has no REST equivalent, so this is the one call that must go through gh's GraphQL-backed --json rather than gh api. Each linked issue's body is then one plain REST call (gh api repos/<repo>/issues/<n>) — typically one issue per PR in this repo's workflow, so the typical run costs 2 calls total.

docs.title: Decision table
docs.text: Situation Result Blocks the PR? PR closes no issue not applicable No Every closed issue declares a surface; files ⊆ union scope OK No Every closed issue declares a surface; a file falls outside, no override violation named Yes Same, but a commit carries surface-override: <reason> OVERRIDDEN + reason logged No At least one closed issue has no surface block UNDECLARED-SURFACE No (see below) The GitHub API is unreadable (rate limit, auth, network) UNKNOWN Yes

docs.title: Strictness: "payable", not "zero current violations"
docs.text:
The issue itself asks which criterion set the strictness, because both look like measurement and answer different questions. This gate picked payable: a linked issue with no declared surface does not block the PR. The alternative — treat an undeclared surface as a violation — would fail every open PR the day this gate merged, since none of the ~40 issues open at the time had a surface block yet (including blueprintx#314 itself). Enforcement activates per issue, the moment that issue's body gets a surface block; there is no separate backfill step to run first.

Known follow-up, stated rather than fabricated: the issue asks to run this gate against origin/main~20..origin/main and report how many merged PRs it would have flagged. That run needs a surface block on each of those merged PRs' issues to mean anything (see the strictness note above) — none exist yet, so the honest number today is "0 issues have a declared surface, so 0 PRs would be flagged and the number says nothing about the gate's real strictness." Re-run it once a meaningful slice of issues have opted in.

docs.title: The override
docs.text:
A PR that must legitimately widen its surface says so, rather than being silently blocked — matching this repo's existing gate-change-ok: convention for a gate a PR must weaken. Add a commit trailer:

surface-override: <reason the PR must touch files outside its issue's declared surface>

on any commit in the PR. The gate still reports every out-of-surface file, but exits 0 with the reason printed alongside them — an override is loud, not invisible.

docs.title: Unreadable API: UNKNOWN, never a silent pass
docs.text: If gh fails (rate limit, auth, network, malformed JSON) at any point — fetching the PR snapshot or an issue body — the check prints ::error::UNKNOWN — could not verify issue scope: <reason> and exits non-zero. This follows the same rule bin/ci/check_actions.sh already applies to a missing actionlint: a gate that goes quiet under a real failure and reports green is a gate reporting its own blindness as OK. An unreadable API is never treated as "no violation found."

docs.title: Feeding this back into dispatch
docs.text: Once a meaningful number of issues carry a surface block, "are issue A and issue B safe to dispatch in parallel" becomes issue_surface(A) ∩ issue_surface(B) == ∅ — a query against two issue bodies, not a prose judgment reconstructed from memory. That wiring (generating an agent's collision map from declared surfaces) is out of scope for this change; it is a natural next step once enough issues declare a surface for the intersection to be meaningful.

docs.title: Not in scope here
docs.text:
• The scope:* label taxonomy from the issue's original proposal, and backfilling it onto existing issues — superseded by the fenced-block design above.
  • Wiring this gate into .pre-commit-config.yaml — a pre-commit hook has no PR or linked-issue context to check against (it runs on a local working tree, not a PR), so there is nothing for it to enforce locally beyond what this PR-time gate already covers.
  • Shipping a copy of this gate into templates/python-common/bin/ for generated projects. It reads this repo's own dispatch conventions (closingIssuesReferences, the surface block convention) via GITHUB_REPOSITORY/PR_NUMBER, the same shape as templates/common/bin/check_review_threads.py — so it travels the same way, if/when a generated project adopts the same per-issue dispatch model. Until then, a second copy nothing exercises is exactly the drift check_test_copy_lists.py/check_actions.sh exist to catch.

docs.title: Lockfile sync gate
docs.text: blueprintx#588, a regression of #464. bin/ci/check_lockfile_sync.sh fails when a templates/*/package.json declares a dependency that its package-lock.json does not carry. That drift is what makes npm ci refuse to install in a generated project.

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
• A pure JSON comparison done with python3, so it runs offline in pre-commit.
  • A tier with no lockfile is skipped, not failed: not every tier ships one.
  • An optional peer dependency need not be installed. It is declared in the lock root and has no node_modules entry, so the gate accepts that shape.
  • Usage: bash bin/ci/check_lockfile_sync.sh [--root <dir>], defaulting to the repo root.

docs.title: The regression test
docs.text: tests/test_check_lockfile_sync.sh covers both directions. A dependency missing from the lock must fail and name the package; a synced pair and a lockfile-less tier must pass. Each case takes a description, the package.json deps, the lock root deps, the lock node_modules keys (space separated, - for a tier without a lockfile), pass or fail, and the needle expected on failure.

docs.title: Dependabot for the ts-lib lockfile
docs.text: .github/dependabot.yml watches /templates/ts-lib because every ts-lib scaffold copies that lockfile (#735). Its eslint group comes first on purpose: the first matching group wins, and @eslint/js moves in lockstep with eslint, majors included.

docs.title: Promoting an offline scaffold to online
docs.text: blueprintx#382. bin/promote_offline_to_online.sh turns an offline-scaffolded project into an online one — a GitHub remote, the GitHub-only CI assets, the branch ruleset — without re-scaffolding and without hand-copying files out of BlueprintX.

docs.title: Why offline mode needs an inverse
docs.text: apply_offline_mode (in every bin/scaffold/python_*.sh and ts_react_app.sh) runs once, at scaffold time, when the developer declines a GitHub remote: GitHub-only assets are skipped, and the offline git-diff workflow is copied in instead. Until this script, the only route back to the online workflow was scaffolding a second project and moving the code across by hand.

docs.title: Why this is a standalone script, not a scaffold change
docs.text: The 5 Python bin/scaffold/python_*.sh scripts and ts_react_app.sh are left untouched on purpose: this script does not source or edit any of them — it transcribes their copy_github_assets / apply_offline_mode manifests instead (see the table below) and runs independently. The one thing it does delegate is the branch ruleset: it runs the project's own bin/enable_repo_rules.sh, shipped at scaffold time, rather than carrying a second copy.

docs.title: Branch protection: the pr-quality-gate ruleset
docs.text:
Generated projects are protected by the pr-quality-gate repository ruleset on the default branch, never by classic branches/<b>/protection. Every scaffold (and this script, on promotion) runs the project's own bin/enable_repo_rules.sh once the remote exists, so the rules are in place from the first push instead of after someone remembers poe enable_repo_rules. Classic protection with required_pull_request_reviews: null used to be applied here, which left a direct push to main open.

The ruleset requires a pull request, blocks force-push and deletion, and requires the contexts listed in bin/required-checks.txt. GitHub forbids self-approval, so the default is 0 required approvals; answering yes to "Will human reviewers gate merges?" at scaffold time sets RULESET_APPROVALS=1. The script is idempotent (it updates the ruleset found by name) and, when rulesets are unavailable (a private repo on a free plan returns 403), it warns loudly and the scaffold continues.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
bin/promote_offline_to_online.sh <project_path> --tier <tier> [options]
Flag Required Meaning <project_path> yes Path to the offline-scaffolded project. --tier yes One of the tiers below. No inference — a wrong guess silently promotes the wrong inventory, so the caller must say which one. --github-user no GitHub owner for the new repo. Default: gh api user. --visibility public\|private no Default private. --deploy-target none\|pages\|vercel no react-spa-webpack only. Default none (see caveat below). --publish none\|pypi\|test-pypi\|both no lib-minimal only. Default none (see caveat below). --skip-branch-protection no Skip running bin/enable_repo_rules.sh (the branch ruleset).

docs.title: What gets added, per tier
docs.text:
The 5 service tiers (ddd-service-native-db, ddd-service-orm-db, mvc-service-native-db, mvc-service-orm-db, api-service-native-db) share one manifest — transcribed from copy_github_assets(), identical across all five:

  • .github/workflows/{tests,review_threads,coderabbit_trigger,review_retry,pr-gate,pr-reconcile,contract_drift,release,docs}.yaml
  • .github/workflows/secret_scan.yaml only when GITGUARDIAN_API_KEY is exported (opt-in, as at scaffold time); the key is set as a repo secret after gh repo create and before the first push, so the first scan has its key. Setting it is best-effort like the ruleset: if it fails the repo is already created and pushed, so the script warns with the exact gh secret set command rather than aborting, and a re-run does nothing
  • .github/CODEOWNERS (envsubst GITHUB_USERNAME, on every tier), .github/CLAUDE.md, .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md, .github/dependabot.yml
  • SECURITY.md (envsubst PROJECT_DISPLAY_NAME, REPOSITORY)

lib-minimal (from lib_minimal_copy_github_assets()) is the same shape minus contract_drift/release, plus docs.yaml from its own templates/lib-minimal/.github/workflows/, plus release-pypi.yaml / release-test-pypi.yaml gated by --publish.

react-spa-webpack (from ts_react_app.sh) ships the templates/ts-common/.github/workflows/ set (build, lint, test, type-check, secret-scan, review-threads) plus .github/CLAUDE.md, .github/CODEOWNERS (envsubst GITHUB_USERNAME), .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md, and — gated by --deploy-target — either deploy-spa.yml or deploy-vercel.yml + vercel.json. No SECURITY.md or dependabot.yml: templates/ts-common/ ships neither.

ts-lib (from ts_lib.sh) ships the same ts-common workflows plus .github/workflows/{docs,docs-deploy,pack-smoke,release-npm}.yml (release-npm.yml rendered with PROJECT_NAME) plus the shared CLAUDE.md, CODEOWNERS and PR template. bash-cli (from bash_cli.sh) ships ci.yml and release.yml (rendered with PROJECT_NAME) plus the same three shared files. Neither ships SECURITY.md, dependabot.yml or secret_scan.yaml. Offline removal is the react one: git-diff trio, git_diffs/ and, where a package.json exists, its git:diff:* scripts.

docs.title: The two "which one was it" gaps
docs.text: Neither the original deploy target (react tier) nor the original publish target (lib-minimal) survives into an offline project — apply_offline_mode removes .github/ entirely for react, and the workflow was simply never written for lib-minimal's unchosen options. This is the same gap the issue names for tier itself ("no doctor artifact... no tier marker persisted"): nothing records the choice, so the script defaults to none rather than guess, and documents the flag instead. Pass --deploy-target / --publish explicitly if the original choice is known.

docs.title: What gets removed (or left, with a warning)
docs.text:
Python tiers: bin/{git_diff_export,git_diff_apply,git_diff_check,new_branch,git_merge_to_main,protect_branch}.sh, poe_tasks.offline.toml (and its entry in poe_tasks.toml's [tool.poe] include list), and the swapped .pre-commit-config.yaml hook — protect-branch (local) is replaced back with the stock no-commit-to-branch. React tier: the git-diff trio and the git:diff:* package.json scripts; react's apply_offline_mode never swapped a pre-commit hook or wired poe, so neither is touched.

git_diffs/ is removed only when it holds nothing but the .keep placeholder apply_offline_mode created — real exported diffs a user actually placed there are left in place with a warning, never silently deleted. bin/lib/common.sh is left alone in every tier: it is not in the offline-only list apply_offline_mode ships, and other tooling may still use it.

docs.title: Preconditions — refuse loudly, never half-promote
docs.text: Checked before any file is touched, in this order: the --tier is one of the known tiers and templates/<tier>/skeleton.meta still exists in this BlueprintX checkout (an unknown or since-removed tier fails loudly rather than copying nothing and reporting success); the tier-specific options are valid; the target is a git repository; not already fully online (an origin remote and .github/CODEOWNERS or a populated .github/workflows/ — that combination is a clean no-op, exit 0); not in the ambiguous state of an origin remote without GitHub assets (refuses — could be mid-promotion or a manually-added remote, and guessing which is exactly what this script exists not to do); the current branch is main (the push and the ruleset both target it); the working tree is clean, unless a previous promotion was interrupted (see below); gh is installed and authenticated. All of these run before any gh call that changes anything.

docs.title: Idempotency and resuming
docs.text:
Every mutation is independently safe to re-run: file copies overwrite identical content, removals use -f/check-first, the poe-include and pre-commit-hook edits detect their own prior application and no-op, and package.json script stripping only rewrites the file when a git:diff:* entry is present. The poe-include and pre-commit-hook edits fail loudly when they find the entry in a shape they do not recognise, rather than reporting success over a half-edited project.

A run interrupted before the first push (most likely: a pre-commit hook rejected the promotion commit) leaves the copied assets in the working tree and no origin. The next run recognises that state — GitHub assets present, no origin — and resumes: it overwrites the workflows from the templates, repeats the removals and commits again. Only the paths this script itself writes or removes may be dirty on a resume; any other uncommitted change is refused. The allowlist is by path, so an uncommitted edit of your own to one of those files (for example package.json) is indistinguishable from the promotion's and is committed with it — stash it first.

After the first push the project reads as online and a re-run does nothing. That includes the ruleset step: it is best-effort, and enable_repo_rules.sh exits 0 even when GitHub refuses, so the script then runs enable_repo_rules.sh verify and reports "NOT in place" unless that exits 0. If it did not, run bash bin/enable_repo_rules.sh yourself with repo-admin rights. What it applies is the same pr-quality-gate ruleset an online scaffold gets: a pull request is required, force-push, deletion and merge commits on main are blocked, and the always-running checks listed in bin/required-checks.txt are required.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
bash -n and shellcheck --severity=warning --exclude=SC1091 pass clean (mirrors CI's shellcheck pre-commit hook). tests/test_promote_offline_to_online.sh exercises the refusal paths (not a git repo, unknown tier, dirty tree, gh unauthenticated, an origin set without GitHub assets), the already-online no-op (including react-spa-webpack with no deploy workflow), and every tier's copy manifest against the real templates/ tree, all against throwaway local git repos with no network or gh auth required.

Not verified here, and stated rather than glossed over: a live round trip (scaffold offline → promote → diff against an online scaffold of the same tier) needs a real gh-authenticated environment with network access to create a repository — the should-fail witness the issue asks for ("diff the two trees and report the count"). That is a manual verification step for whoever runs this against a real project; CI cannot create repositories.

docs.title: Relationship to #109 and #129
docs.text: blueprintx#109 (doctor / template-drift check, open) shares this script's shape — reconcile a scaffolded tree against BlueprintX's current idea of it — but compares against the template where this compares against the online inventory. If #109 lands, promotion could become a mode of it rather than a second walker; until then, keeping this standalone avoids inventing a tier marker or a data-file abstraction (.review-bots.yaml-shaped) for a single consumer. Branch protection is the one piece that is not duplicated: apply_branch_protection delegates to the project's own bin/enable_repo_rules.sh (blueprintx#750).

docs.title: Remote creation order at scaffold time
docs.text:
blueprintx#732. scaffold_create_github_repo (bin/lib/scaffold_git_remote.sh) must not push in the same gh repo create call. The GitGuardian key has to exist before the first push, or the first secret_scan run on main of every new repo goes red, so the order is create, set the key, then push.

  • gh repo create is called without --push, and without --source/--remote either: origin is already added, and gh fails on an existing remote.
  • When create fails because the repo already exists, the function returns 0 so the caller's create-failed fallback does not run again. That fallback pushes itself, key first.
  • On success the create step has already set the scan key before its push.
  • A failed first push leaves no upstream, so the prompt returns non-zero and callers skip branch protection rather than protect a branch that is not there.
  • tests/test_scaffold_git_remote.sh makes the order observable with a logging gh stub and a local bare remote: the stub records whether main already exists on the remote when the secret is set. It covers the ok path, the existing-remote fallback and the failed-push path.

docs.title: Offline Wheelhouse
docs.text:
How a scaffolded Python project installs its dependencies on a machine that cannot reach PyPI at all — a corporate box behind a TLS-inspecting proxy that blocks the index outright, not merely one that needs its CA trusted. Ships in every Python skeleton via templates/python-common/bin/build_wheelhouse.sh (blueprintx#299, pieces 1-3 of #127).

See also: Troubleshooting for the corporate-CA half of this problem · FAQ.

docs.title: Why this exists
docs.text:
poe venv already fails loudly on a blocked index instead of silently leaving an empty .venv behind (verify_venv_imports.py, blueprintx#127 piece 4). Failing loudly names the problem; it does not fix it. When the index is genuinely unreachable — not just untrusted — the only remedy is to bring the wheels with you.

Two probes that lie, worth repeating because both were the actual cause the first time this was measured:

  • curl reaching pypi.org proves nothing about pip. A reachable host and a usable package index are different questions.
  • A pip install that never needed --upgrade never queried the index. A probe package already satisfied locally passes even when the network is fully blocked.

docs.title: Building the wheelhouse (on a machine WITH internet access)
docs.text:
poe wheelhouse

In VS Code, the same step is the wheelhouse entry in the Tasks menu (and wheelhouse_assemble for the target-side step below).

This writes a sibling payload — ../_wheels/<repo-name>/, one level outside the project — never inside it: code changes constantly, wheels almost never, and a payload inside the repo would be a git add candidate and would not survive a re-clone. It is per-repo because sibling projects pin different versions.

Three steps, run in order:

  1. Export the locked, marker-annotated dependency set via poe export_deps's own poetry export (reused, not reimplemented).
  2. Select — evaluate each requirement's PEP 508 marker against a TARGET environment, not the build machine's own. pip download --platform does not do this: it evaluates markers against the CURRENT interpreter, so a Linux build downloading for a Windows target silently drops pywin32 (declared with markers = "sys_platform == 'win32'") with no error. This step also prunes whichever DB driver DB_BACKEND did not select — the native-DB tiers ship pyodbc/oracledb/psycopg/mysql-connector-python unconditionally (the backend is chosen at runtime from config, not at scaffold time), so shipping all four in the wheelhouse is pure waste (measured 65 MB → 45 MB).
  3. Pack — zip the downloaded wheels, split into fixed-size parts, and write manifest.json recording every part's sha256 plus the whole archive's sha256. A truncated cat of 1-of-5 parts otherwise writes a zip whose only symptom is End-of-central-directory signature not found — a message naming nothing useful. The manifest is what lets the install side catch that before writing a broken archive.

docs.title: Targeting a different machine than the one you're building on
docs.text:
Unset, the wheelhouse targets the build machine's own Python version, platform and architecture — the common case (build and target are the same OS, only the network differs). Override any of these to build for a different target:

Variable Default Meaning WHEELHOUSE_DIR ../_wheels/<repo-name> Where the payload is written WHEELHOUSE_TARGET_PYTHON_VERSION build machine's Target python_version for marker evaluation WHEELHOUSE_TARGET_SYS_PLATFORM build machine's Target sys.platform (win32/linux/darwin) WHEELHOUSE_TARGET_PLATFORM_MACHINE build machine's Target platform.machine() (x86_64, AMD64, ...) WHEELHOUSE_TARGET_IMPLEMENTATION cpython Target Python implementation WHEELHOUSE_PIP_PLATFORM unset pip's own --platform tag (win_amd64, manylinux2014_x86_64, ...) — needed only for a genuinely cross-platform binary download; see below WHEELHOUSE_PIP_ABI unset pip's own --abi tag, paired with WHEELHOUSE_PIP_PLATFORM WHEELHOUSE_PART_MB 45 Split-part size DB_BACKEND unset postgresql/mysql/mariadb/oracle/mssql — prunes the other native-DB drivers (see the install caveat below)

WHEELHOUSE_TARGET_* only changes which packages are selected (the marker-evaluation step). It does not by itself make pip fetch a binary wheel built for a different platform — that needs WHEELHOUSE_PIP_PLATFORM too, using pip's own platform-tag vocabulary (deliberately not re-derived here; see pip's own --platform docs). Most users building and installing on the same OS never need to set it.

docs.title: Transferring the payload
docs.text: Copy ../_wheels/<repo-name>/ (USB drive, internal file share, whatever the corporate network policy allows) so it sits beside the offline clone of the project — the same sibling relationship it was built in.

docs.title: Assembling and installing (on the OFFLINE target)
docs.text:
poe wheelhouse_assemble
pip install --no-index --find-links ../_wheels/<repo-name>/wheels -r requirements-lock.txt

poe itself comes from PyPI, so it may be missing on the offline target. The task only runs bash bin/build_wheelhouse.sh assemble, which you can call directly.

⚠️ If you built with DB_BACKEND set, do not install with -r requirements-lock.txt. The lock file still names the pruned drivers, and --no-index cannot fetch them, so pip fails with No matching distribution found. Install the wheel set itself instead — it is a complete dependency closure:

pip install --no-index --find-links ../_wheels/<repo-name>/wheels ../_wheels/<repo-name>/wheels/*.whl

wheelhouse_assemble accepts three payload shapes, tried in order, and REFUSES rather than writing a broken result:

  1. Loose wheels already sitting in the output directory — nothing to do.
  2. Manifest + split parts (what poe wheelhouse produces) — every part's presence and sha256 is checked against manifest.json before concatenation, and the reassembled archive's own sha256 is checked again before extraction. A missing part, a part-count mismatch, or a single corrupted byte aborts with a named cause instead of silently producing a truncated wheels/ directory.
  3. A bare wheelhouse.zip with no manifest — accepted as-is (e.g. someone zipped the wheels/ folder by hand for a quick transfer); there is nothing to verify it against, so this path is explicitly unverified.

docs.title: Should-fail witness
docs.text:
Verified against an actually blocked index, not merely an absent one — a reachable-but-empty index still looks like success to a probe that never asked for the right thing:

poe wheelhouse_assemble
dir_witness="$(mktemp -d)" && python -m venv "$dir_witness"   # fresh: nothing pre-installed
PIP_INDEX_URL=http://127.0.0.1:1/simple "$dir_witness/bin/pip" install --find-links ../_wheels/<repo-name>/wheels -r requirements-lock.txt

The venv must be fresh: in an environment that already holds the requirements, pip is satisfied locally and passes without ever reading the wheelhouse, so a missing wheel goes unnoticed (the second probe that lies, above).

The command deliberately omits --no-index: with it pip never contacts PIP_INDEX_URL, so the unreachable index would prove nothing. Without it, a wheel missing from the wheelhouse falls through to the blocked index and the install fails, which is the property this section witnesses. The install must succeed with the network fully denied. A wheelhouse that is never exercised this way is not verified — it is a directory.

docs.title: Repo policy workflows
docs.text:
Scaffolded GitHub repos carry six server-side PR/issue policies in .github/workflows/ (blueprintx#604). Local hooks only guard one machine; these run for every contributor. Offline scaffolds (no GitHub remote) do not receive them.

Workflow Rule close-linked-issues.yml On a merged same-repo PR into the default branch, closes the issues named by the branch (<type>/<N>-<slug>) or by Closes/Fixes/Resolves #N. branch-has-issue.yml Fails a PR whose head branch carries no issue number (<type>/<N>-<slug>). release/, dependabot/ and renovate/ branches are exempt. pr-title-conventional.yml Fails a PR title that is not a Conventional Commit; squash merges use it as the commit subject. pr-body-template.yml Fails a PR body missing a ## section of .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md. pr-self-assign.yml Assigns the author when a same-repo PR is opened. dependabot-auto-merge.yml Arms auto-merge for Dependabot patch/minor bumps; majors wait for a review. See Dependabot auto-merge.

The checks run bin/check_pr_policy.sh, copied into the project (never fetched at run time). Untrusted branch, title and body text reaches the scripts through env: only.

Moving cards to In progress / In review is out of scope: GITHUB_TOKEN cannot write a user-owned Projects v2 board, so that stays in a local hook or behind a PAT secret.

docs.title: Design notes
docs.text:
• The three check workflows run on pull_request_target, so the workflow definition, the script and the template all come from the base branch and a PR cannot rewrite the check that judges it. They never check out PR code: branch, title and body arrive through env: from the event only. Bot authors (user.type == 'Bot') are skipped.
  • check_pr_policy.sh takes BRANCH, TITLE or BODY (plus TEMPLATE, default .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md) from the environment and exits 0 (pass), 1 (violation) or 2 (bad usage). Sourcing it defines the functions without running them, which the tests use.
  • A trailing -<N> in a branch name is not an issue number (chore/bump-node-20 is a version).
  • pr-self-assign.yml skips fork PRs (read-only token) and needs only pull-requests: write.
  • The new check names are deliberately absent from each tier's bin/required-checks.txt, which allows a name only after a real PR has emitted it. Add them once they have reported.
  • Offline scaffolds drop .github/ but keep close_linked_issues.sh and check_pr_policy.sh in bin/, and drop dependabot_auto_merge.sh (tracked in #727).

docs.title: Scaffold prompts and non-terminal stdin
docs.text: blueprintx#539. Every interactive y/n question the scaffolds ask goes through prompt_yes_no in bin/lib/common.sh. Nothing in a scaffold or its libs reads stdin for a prompt without passing the prompt_can_read guard.

docs.title: Why the guard exists
docs.text:
read consumes a non-terminal stdin without complaint. A non-interactive run (CI, --dev, a stray line left on a pipe) would therefore answer a question nobody asked. For an opt-in such as OTEL that means dependencies installed and files rewritten with nobody agreeing to it.

With no terminal on stdin, the variable is set to the prompt's default without ever calling read, so a leftover y on the pipe can never flip an unattended run.

docs.title: The helpers
docs.text: Helper Behavior prompt_can_read True when stdin may answer a prompt: a terminal, or a harness that feeds answers on purpose by exporting BLUEPRINTX_STDIN_ANSWERS=1 (the bin/lib/spec.sh pipes). A stray piped line without that opt-in is never an answer. prompt_warn_default <prompt> [label] One stderr line saying a prompt fell back to its default because stdin is not a terminal. Stdout and exit status are untouched. prompt_read <var> <prompt> [label] read -r -p that leaves the variable empty, so the caller's own default applies, when prompt_can_read is false or stdin is at EOF. Without a readable stdin it also warns on stderr. prompt_yes_no <var> "$(prompt_main "Question? [y/N]: ")" [y\|n] Sets the variable to the literal true or false, the convention every INCLUDE_* / USE_* flag already uses. The prompt argument is fully rendered by the caller, so the helper stays agnostic to styling.

docs.title: Choosing the default
docs.text:
The default is chosen per prompt, not globally. Hardcoding one default would trade one silent wrong answer for another.

An opt-in defaults to n: installing dependencies or sending telemetry must never happen silently. The one exception is a prompt whose safe unattended answer is yes, such as waiting for the first deploy to finish after a confirmed Pages setup: it is a passive poll, not a mutation, so it passes y.

Prompt Default Reason Branch protection n A GitHub API mutation (enforce_admins, required checks); an unattended run must not lock down a repo nobody confirmed. Required reviews n Matches the pre-existing fallback: a solo maintainer with no required reviews. Database Compose stack n Ships a whole database stack nobody asked for. Schema-less storage n Adds a storage backend and chassis code. Output layout n Changing the on-disk output layout must never happen silently; the fallback stays flat and not date-organised. Webhook notifications n Adds outbound network calls to a platform nobody named. E-mail sending n Same reasoning as webhooks. OTEL n Installs telemetry dependencies and sends data to a collector; originally fixed inline in #519, now folded into the shared helper. Multi-pipeline n Opt-in, default No; generates a whole dispatch trio nobody asked for. MULTI_PIPELINE_OPTIN=true is the sanctioned non-interactive override. Config directory layout n Environment-wise config silently changes the on-disk shape of the generated project; an unattended run gets the single-file layout that pressing Enter gives. Module Federation n Reshapes webpack.config.js; an unattended run must not pick a different build topology. Dockerfile and nginx n Adds files nobody asked for. Delivery script n Ships an extra script plus package.json entries. Enable GitHub Pages n A GitHub API mutation; an unattended run must not publish a site nobody confirmed. Wait for the first deploy y Passive poll after a confirmed Pages setup.

The GitHub username, the React variant and the deploy target are not y/n prompts. With no terminal the read is skipped, so a stray pipe line cannot answer as a username or pick a variant or target nobody chose; they fall straight to DEFAULT_GITHUB_USERNAME and to the 1 default.

docs.title: The regression test
docs.text:
tests/test_prompt_tty_guard.sh has three legs.

  • The helpers behave: a piped y is not an answer unless the harness opted in.
  • The warning leg: piped without the opt-in, the fallback is announced on stderr only; with the opt-in nothing is printed there. A terminal cannot be simulated in the test, so that leg is covered by the opted-in assertion, which takes the same read path.
  • The static leg: any bare read prompt in a scaffold or its libs must sit directly under a prompt_can_read guard. while ... read loops over files are not prompts.

docs.title: DDD Service — Native DB (Domain-Driven Design, hexagonal service)
docs.text:
A Domain-Driven Design scaffold with a hexagonal (ports-and-adapters) layout. It keeps business logic isolated from I/O while allowing shared infrastructure when it is truly cross-cutting.

This template uses native database libraries (psycopg, sqlite3, oracledb, pyodbc, mysql-connector-python, etc.) for direct database access, giving you fine-grained control over queries and connections. For schema-less persistence the same DatabaseHandler contract covers JSON, CSV, and joblib backends via chassis/db_wschema/ — added only if you opt into schema-less storage at scaffold time (declined by default).

Examples: External API Calls · Wiring with FastAPI · Bank Balance Alert

docs.title: 🗂️ Expected layout (after scaffold)
docs.text:

  src/
    app/
      bootstrap.py          # env loading, logging, elapsed-time tracking
      container.py          # composition root — AppContainer
    capabilities/<feature>/
      domain/               # entities.py · dto.py · enums.py · ports.py
      application/          # use_cases.py · factories.py
      infrastructure/       # repositories.py
    chassis/
      db/
        domain/ports.py             # DatabaseHandler ABC + Record type
        infrastructure/helpers.py   # ensure_id helper
      db_schema/
        domain/entities.py
        application/database_factory.py   # build_database_handler()
        infrastructure/
          sqlite_handler.py
          postgres_handler.py
          mariadb_handler.py
          mysql_handler.py
          mssql_handler.py
          oracle_handler.py
      db_wschema/                         # optional — added only if you opt into schema-less storage
        application/storage_factory.py    # build_storage_handler()
        infrastructure/
          json_handler.py
          csv_handler.py
          joblib_handler.py
          sanity_check.py
      typing/
        abc_type_checker.py
        protocol_type_checker.py

      startup.py            # logger, webhooks, runtime constants (module-level singletons)
      inputs.yaml
